summary: This note is an excerpt of RFC 2616 (HTTP/1.1) section 14, which defines the syntax and semantics of standard HTTP/1.1 header fields. It covers the request headers Accept, Accept-Charset, Accept-Encoding and Accept-Language, the response headers Accept-Ranges and Age, the entity-header Allow, the request header Authorization, and the general-header Cache-Control with its cacheability, storage and expiration directives. The clipped text ends partway through section 14.9.4 on cache revalidation and reload controls.
one_line: Excerpt of RFC 2616 section 14 defining HTTP/1.1 header fields such as Accept, Authorization, Age and Cache-Control.
key_facts: RFC 2616 section 14 is titled "Header Field Definitions" and defines the syntax and semantics of all standard HTTP/1.1 header fields.
The Accept request-header field specifies media types acceptable for the response, and the default quality value is q=1.
The example Accept: audio/*; q=0.2, audio/basic means the client prefers audio/basic but will accept any audio type after an 80% mark-down in quality.
If no Accept header field is present, the client is assumed to accept all media types, and the server SHOULD send a 406 (not acceptable) response when it cannot satisfy the Accept header.
In Accept-Charset, the special value "*" matches every character set not mentioned elsewhere in the field.
The Accept-Encoding rules state that the identity content-coding is always acceptable unless refused by identity;q=0 or *;q=0.
The Accept-Language field assigns a language quality factor based on the longest matching language-range, and assigns 0 if no range matches.
Accept-Ranges: bytes indicates a server accepts byte-range requests, and Accept-Ranges: none advises clients not to attempt range requests.
The Age header value must be non-negative decimal integers in seconds, and a cache that overflows must transmit an Age value of 2147483648 (2^31).
An Allow header field MUST be present in a 405 (Method Not Allowed) response, and a proxy MUST NOT modify the Allow header field.
A user agent sends an Authorization request-header field with credentials, usually after receiving a 401 response.
A shared cache must not return a response to an Authorization request for another request, except under specific exceptions involving s-maxage, must-revalidate or public.
The Cache-Control directive no-store is meant to prevent the inadvertent release or retention of sensitive information, such as on backup tapes.
The max-age directive overrides the Expires header even when the Expires header is more restrictive.
